questions.q: A wireframe is best described as:
choices: The final, fully styled version of a screen
A low-fidelity sketch of a screen's layout and content, without visual design
A type of database schema
A piece of server-side code
questions.explanation: Wireframes are a two-dimensional sketch of a screen's layout, prioritizing space and content over visual design. They let everyone walk through structure and functionality early, surfacing questions cheaply instead of expensively later in development.

questions.q: In the fidelity spectrum, what comes right after a low-fidelity wireframe?
choices: A sketch
A mockup
A finished, deployed page
A database migration
questions.explanation: The spectrum runs Sketch → Wireframe → Mockup → Prototype. A mockup adds real colors, fonts, and imagery on top of the structure a wireframe already established.

questions.q: What's the purpose of an X-box placeholder in a wireframe?
choices: It marks a section that should be deleted
It stands in for an image that doesn't exist yet, without distracting from the layout conversation
It indicates a broken link
It shows where a database query will run
questions.explanation: An X-box (a rectangle with a diagonal cross) is shared wireframe shorthand for "an image goes here" — it reserves the right amount of space without anyone reacting to actual photography or artwork that isn't ready yet.

questions.q: What's the key difference between a mockup and a prototype?
choices: A mockup is clickable and a prototype is static
A prototype simulates interaction (clicking through a flow); a mockup is a static, fully styled image
They are two names for the same thing
A prototype has no visual design at all
questions.explanation: A mockup is a static, high-fidelity image of one screen. A prototype links multiple mockups together so someone can click through an actual flow — sign up, confirm, land on the dashboard — before any code exists.

questions.q: Why present a wireframe as explicitly "not final design"?
choices: To avoid legal liability
So stakeholders don't fixate on colors and fonts during a structure conversation
Because wireframes are always thrown away afterward
Because clients aren't allowed to see wireframes
questions.explanation: Skipping this reminder is one of the most common ways a structure conversation accidentally turns into a color-palette argument. Naming the stage out loud keeps the conversation focused on what it's actually meant to cover.
